Stated Claim / Post Context:
Tusla reported seven companies that run children’s homes to Gardaí over Garda-vetting concerns

“Any organisation that does not rigorously enforce Garda vetting for every adult working with children is failing in its fundamental duty of care," says Terry Dignan, of the Children's Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association.

Actual Article Body:

Like, what'll be the route to dig up the footpath and lay down a wire?

“Any organisation that does not rigorously enforce Garda vetting for every adult working with children is failing in its fundamental duty of care," says Terry Dignan, of the Children's Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association.

Between 2023 and 2025, Tusla reported seven private companies that run children’s homes to Gardaí, due to suspected issues with Garda vetting, according to a disclosures table released under the Freedom of Information Act.

While it is a criminal offence to employ a person who is not Garda vetted in a role that requires vetting, those situations, when identified, are not always referred to Gardaí.

The issues that Tusla referred to Gardaí were described in the disclosures table as either “suspicion of falsification of vetting document” or a “irregularity in Garda vetting received.”

Last year, a staff member at Good People Homecare and a company director of Ideal Care – were convicted of falsifying documents related to Garda vetting, after Tusla referred issues to Gardaí in 2023.

Garda vetting is a process that allows an employer to check whether a person has certain convictions, such as violent crimes or sexual offences before employing them to work directly with children.

Ideal Care Services admitted submitting false or misleading background checks to Tusla including “altered” Garda vetting documents, false staff references and falsified records of reference checks, according to an Irish Times report.

An employee of Good People was convicted of 55 counts of forging Garda vetting certs, according to the Irish Times.

“Garda vetting is a mandatory statutory mechanism and a foundational pillar of child protection in Irish residential care,” says Terry Dignan, of the Children's Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association (CRAVA).

Because residential care environments cater to highly vulnerable children who have often experienced prior trauma, rigorous background screening can provide an initial barrier against the potential risk of abuse, he says.

Those companies that have failed on vetting should not be allowed to continue to profit from caring for vulnerable children, says Dignan.

“Any organisation that does not rigorously enforce Garda vetting for every adult working with children is failing in its fundamental duty of care and is not, in my opinion, an organisation that should be involved in the care of children,” he says.

“Vetting is the first line of defence in the protection of children in care,” says Wayne Stanley, CEO of the advocacy organisation Empowering Young People in Care (EPIC).

“If that basic standard is not met or avoided, that would be a breach of trust that EPIC would believe it is difficult to move past,” he said.

As of February this year, Tusla was still contracting – to look after children – at least four of the seven companies which it had referred to Gardaí over suspected vetting issues between 2023 and 2025.

That is according to a list of registered children’s homes providers presented in the Dáil, by the Minister for Children, Norma Foley, in February 2026.

One of the companies that was still running registered homes, was reported for “suspicion of falsification of vetting document” in 2023 and 2024, according to the disclosures table. A spokesperson for Tusla wouldn't comment on the current status of particular cases.

“Where we have significant cause for concern, such as suspected fraud or serious wrongdoing, Tusla will refer it to An Garda Síochána (AGS) without delay,” says a spokesperson.
